etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 御 (o-, polite prefix) +‎ 菓子 (kashi, “confection”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御(お) (o-, beautifying prefix) + 金(かね) (kane, “money”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
/itɨ/ → /it͡sɨ/ → /it͡ɕɨ/
From Middle Chinese 一 (ʔiɪt̚).
Compare modern Hokkien 一 (it).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text:
/itʉ/ → /it͡sʉ/ → /it͡su/
From Middle Chinese 一 (ʔiɪt̚).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3 2
etymologies.text:
/pʲitə/ → ⟨pi1to2⟩ → /ɸito/ → /hito/
From Old Japanese 一 (pi1to2), from earlier Proto-Japonic *pitə. Cognate with Okinawan 一 (tī)
Related to 二 (futa, “two”), which is its double. Compare 三 (mi, “three”) and 六 (mu, “six”), 四 (yo, “four”) and 八 (ya, “eight”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4 2
etymologies.text: Shortening of hito above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: Long-pronounced form of hi above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 6
etymologies.text: Borrowing from Mandarin 一 (yī) in the Qing Dynasty.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 7
etymologies.text: From 始(はじ)め (hajime, “beginning, first”), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 始(はじ)める (hajimeru, “to begin”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By surface analysis, 事務(じむ) (jimu) + 所(しょ) (-sho).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *ima. Frellesvig suggests a compound of reconstructed proximal demonstrative *i (compare Middle Korean 이 (i, “this”)) + ma (corresponding to modern 間(ま) (ma, “space”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 今 (MC kim).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tukoru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ki1ru⟩ → */kjiru/ → /kiru/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kiru. Cognate with Miyako 切 (きぃー, ksïï), Okinawan 切ーん (ちーん, chīn), Yaeyama 切すん (きぃすん, kïsun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Attributed to Old Japanese, although the exact phonetics are not clear, as the term is not cited in phonetic man'yōgana.
Ultimate derivation unknown.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Mandarin 北 (běi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: (This term, 北, is a variant kanji form of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Two possible sources:
From a nominalization of the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “terminal form”) or 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) of the verb 向(む)かう (mukau, “to face”). The modern pronunciation would suggest that the morpheme boundary in the original verb muka.u has been lost.
From a nominalization of the ウ音(おん)便(びん) (u-onbin, “u euphonic change”) form of 向(む)かい (mukai, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 向(む)かう (mukau, “to face”)), compare dialectal forms like 向(む)こうて (mukōte).
Accordingly, the historical kana spellings should be むかふ (mukafu) according to the former, and むかう (mukau) according to the latter. Compare 相撲(すもう) (sumō), of similar derivation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 売(う)り (uri, “selling”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 売(う)る (uru, “to sell”)) + 場(ば) (ba, “place”).
Attested since at least 1595.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɡwaikokuzin/ → /ɡaikokudʑin/
By surface analysis, 外国(がいこく) (gaikoku, “foreign country”) + 人(じん) (-jin, “person”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *əpə. Cognate with 大きい (ōkii, “big, large”) and Proto-Ryukyuan *opo (whence Okinawan 多さん (ufusan)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
⟨womi1na⟩ → */womʲina/ → /womʉna/ → /wonːa/ → /onːa/
Shift from Old Japanese womina → omina. See the 女 (omina) entry for further details.
Now one of the standard Japanese words for "a woman".

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text:
⟨womi1na⟩ → */womʲina/ → /omina/
From Old Japanese.
The initial /wo/ expressed "small, youth" and contrasted with /o/ "grown, old" (as in 嫗 (omina, “old woman”)), while the medial /mi/ is cognate with 女 (me, “female, woman”, see below). According to Frellesvig (2010), proto-Japonic /e/ became Old Japanese [je] in final position and [i] elsewhere; analogous with PJ /o/, which became OJ [wo] in final position and [u] elsewhere (though PJ /i/ and /u/ also existed, compare Old Japanese 火's two readings /po/ & /pu/ in Western & Eastern Old Japanese, respectively (Vovin, 2017)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3 2
etymologies.text:
⟨me1⟩ → */mʲe/ → /me/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mia.
Appears to be distinct from 目 (⟨me2⟩ → me, “eye”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
⟨womi1na⟩ → */womʲina/ → /womʉna/ → /woũna/ → /woːna/ → /oːna/
Variant shift from Old Japanese womina → omina (see above).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
/wonːa/ → /wona/ → /ona/
Shift from onna (see above).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 6
etymologies.text:
/wona/ → /wonaː/ → /onaː/
Long-pronounced form of ona (see above).

/dɨo/ → /d͡ʑo/
From Middle Chinese 女 (MC nrjoX|nrjoH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 8
etymologies.text: (This term, 女, is an alternative spelling (rare, kanbun) of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Probably related to 堅い / 硬い / 固い (katai, “hard”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Derived from kata above. The kata changes to gata as an instance of rendaku (連濁). Found most commonly as a suffixing element in compounds.
The standalone noun sense was originally a shortening of 女形 (onnagata, literally “woman form”), a female role played by a male actor in kabuki theater. This noun sense is only spelled with the 形 kanji.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Compound of 形 (kata, “shape, form”) +‎ ち (-chi), but the derivation of the chi element is unclear.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 形 (MC heng). Compare modern Mandarin 形 (xíng). The 漢音(かんおん) (kan'on) reading, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
From 成り (nari), the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of the verb 成る (naru, “to become”).
First attested as a suffix on a noun in the 曾我物語 (Soga Mongatari), of uncertain dating but probably in the late 1300s. As a suffix on a verb stem, first attested from 1927.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sankasu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 次 (MC tshijH, “in order; second”).
Less common reading in modern Japanese. Superseded in most cases by ji; see below.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text:
/si/ → /ʑi/ → /d͡ʑi/
Sound shift from shi above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3 2
etymologies.text: Nominalization of the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of Old Japanese-derived verb 次ぐ (tsugu, “to be in a sequence; to follow, to continue from something, to be next; to connect, to join”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4 2
etymologies.text:
Nominalization of the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of Old Japanese-derived verb 次く (suku, “to follow, to continue from something, to be next;”).
The verb form was obsolete even in olden times. Existence of the verb, possibly related to tsugu mentioned above, is inferred from placenames found in the Man'yōshū and other ancient poetry.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
/tuɡite/ → /tuide/
Sound shift from 次第 (tsugite, “order, sequence”), itself originally the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of now-obsolete Old Japanese-derived verb 継ぎつ (tsugitsu, “to do things in sequence, to establish an order”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:海
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Sea
Wikipedia
English Wikipedia has an article on:Ocean
Wikipedia
⟨umi1⟩ → */umij/ → /umi/
From Old Japanese, theorized as descending from Proto-Japonic *omi.
Has been thought to have been derived from a compound. There are two leading theories regarding the ultimate derivation:
Shift from 大 (ō-, “big, great”) + 水 (mi, “water”, combining form).
This is problematic phonetically because there is no known term having a related shift from /opo/ → /oː/ → /o/ → /u/, and semantically as there already exists a compound 大水 (ōmizu, “flood”).
From う (u-, stem indicating “ocean”) + 水 (mi, “water”, combining form). The u- stem is evident in 魚 (uo, “fish”) and 潮 (ushio, “salt water; tide”), and in the 海 (una) element in various ancient terms (see below).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Thought to be comprised of う (u-, stem indicating “ocean”) + な (na, ancient alternative form of the possessive particle の (no)). The u- stem is also evident in 魚 (uo, “fish”) and 潮 (ushio, “salt water; tide”).
First cited to the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
Probably related to Korean 바다 (bada, “ocean, sea”); perhaps an ancient Koreanic borrowing into Japanese. Other theories include a connection to 遠 (woti → ochi, woto → oto, “distant place”) or to 渡る (wataru, “to cross, to ford”).
Also read as wada.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Either cognate with 水 (mi, “water”), or an abbreviation of umi above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 海 (MC xojX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 涼し (sususi, suzusi, “cold, refreshing, cool”), following シク活用 (shiku katsuyō, “-shiku conjugation”). First cited to the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, and the Man'yōshū, completed sometime after 759 CE.
May ultimately derive from onomatopoeia. Compare 涼む (suzumu, “to cool down”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Genkan on Wikipedia
/ɡenkwan/ → /ɡenkan/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From earlier genkan. genkwan > genkwa > genka. The final /a/ was likely nasalized. Common during the Edo period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 留学(りゅうがく) (ryūgaku) + 生(せい) (-sei)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From 病(びょう) (byō, “illness”) + 院(いん) (-in, “institution”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The causative form of verb 知る (shiru, “to know”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Derived from the tashi- element seen in たしに (tashi ni, “sufficiently; firmly; surely”) and たしない (tashinai, “difficult, agonizing; poor, lacking”) + adjective-forming suffix か (-ka).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/we/ → /e/
From Middle Chinese 繪 (MC hwajH). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.
Compare Wu 繪 / 绘 (6we).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 繪 (MC hwajH). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 美(うつく)し (utsukushi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in しき (shiki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of しい (shii). Most likely related to 厳しい (itsukushii, “beautiful, pretty”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 美しい, is an alternative spelling (rare) of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: (This term, 美しい, is an alternative spelling (uncommon) of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
/iɕi/ → /iɕiki/ → /iɕiː/
From Early Middle Japanese adjective 美(い)し (ishi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in しき (shiki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of しい (shii). The ishii form appears in informal spoken use from roughly the 1200s-1300s, persisting through the Edo period. In turn, the base form 美し (ishi) is first attested from the early 1200s.
Speculatively, may be derived from or otherwise related to 良い (yoi) / 良い (ii, “good”). Compare what may be a similar "y" ↔ "i" alternation in pairs such as 夢 (ime) / 夢 (yume, “dream”), 稲 (ine, “rice plant”) / 米 (yone, “rice”).
The delicious sense appears to have grown out of 女房詞 (nyōbō kotoba, “woman's word”) usage from the late 1300s, when this word was used primarily by women to express that food was particularly "good". Feminine usage patterns also led to the inclusion of the honorific prefix お- (o-), leading to modern term 美味しい (oishii, “delicious”) as a more polite synonym to うまい (umai, “delicious”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/pana/ → /fana/ → /hana/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pana.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Early Middle Japanese adjective 苦(にが)し (nigashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *ninka; cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *niga.
First cited to a text from 858.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 車 (MC tsyhae).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū completed some time after 759 CE, with the ideographic spelling 車. Also attested in the 正倉院文書 (Shōsō-in Bunsho) set of documents dated to the Nara period, appearing in the phonetic (man'yōgana) spelling of 久流末 (kuruma).
Assuming an initial meaning of wheel, may be a compound of くる (kuru, related to spinning or rotating, as in 繰る (kuru, “to spin (as in thread)”), 枢 (kuru, “hinge”), くるくる (kurukuru, “spinningly, round and round”), 転めく (kurumeku, “to spin round and round, to rotate; to be dizzy”)) +‎ ま (ma, a suffix added to various parts of speech to form an indeclinable word indicating state).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 逃ぐ (nigu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *nink-ai-.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/d͡ʑikidoː/ → /ɕokudoː/
Shift from older reading jikidō (“refectory in a Buddhist temple”). In the Meiji period, the pronunciation shifted to using the kan'on reading of shoku for 食 as the sense expanded to indicate dining facilities in a dormitory, and from there, to any larger room for serving or selling food to multiple people.
First attested in 1903.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/d͡ʑikidau/ → /d͡ʑikidɔː/ → /d͡ʑikidoː/
From Middle Chinese 食堂 (MC zyik dang). First attested in 747.
